title: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
summary: One Converse call for many models, token quotas and max_tokens, on-demand vs provisioned capacity with worked numbers, customization paths, managed building blocks, and the Trainium and Inferentia layer.
outcomes: Explain how the Converse API normalizes requests and responses across models and how to handle each stopReason
Compute start-of-request and final TPM quota usage and explain why an oversized max_tokens causes throttling
Compute when Provisioned Throughput beats on-demand from peak load, Model Unit size and utilization
Choose between fine-tuning, reinforcement fine-tuning, distillation, continued pre-training and import, and say where LoRA fits
Describe what Inferentia, Trainium and Neuron are for and when SageMaker AI fits better than Bedrock

lessons.title: One API in front of many models: the Converse call

blocks.md:
Amazon Bedrock is a fully managed AWS service that gives you API access to foundation models from many providers. A *foundation model* (FM) is a large pretrained model, such as an LLM, that you use as is or adapt.

The naive way to use several models is to call each one with its own request format. On Bedrock that is the `InvokeModel` operation: its body is model-specific JSON, so the fields for one provider's model do not work for another. Switching models then means rewriting request building, response parsing and token accounting.

The **Converse API** (`Converse`, and `ConverseStream` for streaming) fixes the shape. The AWS docs describe it as "a consistent API that works with all Amazon Bedrock models that support messages", so you write the code once and change only the `modelId`.

It lives on the `bedrock-runtime` endpoint. Model-specific knobs that are not in the common set go into a separate field, `additionalModelRequestFields`, instead of breaking the common shape.

blocks.title: From one adapter per model to one call shape

scenes.caption: Naive: the app builds a different JSON body per model provider. Every new model means a new adapter and new parsing code.
Converse: the app sends one message shape to bedrock-runtime. Only the modelId changes.
The same modelId slot also accepts an inference profile (cross-Region routing), a Provisioned Throughput ARN or a custom model deployment ARN.
It also accepts a prompt router ARN. The router picks a model per request; your code is unchanged.

blocks.code:
import boto3
client = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime", region_name="us-east-1")

resp = client.converse(
    modelId=MODEL_ID,  # base model, inference profile, or an ARN
    system=[{"text": "You are a support assistant. Answer briefly."}],
    messages=[
        {"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "How do I reset my password?"}]},
    ],
    inferenceConfig={"maxTokens": 400, "temperature": 0.2, "topP": 0.9},
    additionalModelRequestFields={"top_k": 50},  # only if this model supports it
)
print(resp["output"]["message"]["content"][0]["text"])
print(resp["stopReason"], resp["usage"], resp["metrics"]["latencyMs"])
blocks.caption: A Converse call. inferenceConfig holds the four common parameters (maxTokens, stopSequences, temperature, topP); anything else goes in additionalModelRequestFields. The AWS docs use top_k as their example of such a field.

blocks.md:
The response is a normalized envelope. The docs say Converse "drop[s] most model-native fields by default" and returns `output`, `stopReason`, `usage` and `metrics`:

- `output.message`: the assistant message, a list of content blocks (text, tool use, and so on).
- `stopReason`: why generation stopped. Documented values include `end_turn`, `tool_use`, `max_tokens`, `stop_sequence`, `guardrail_intervened` and `content_filtered`.
- `usage`: `inputTokens`, `outputTokens`, `totalTokens`, plus cache read and write counts when prompt caching is on.
- `metrics.latencyMs`: server-side latency of the call.

If you need a provider field that was dropped, list its JSON Pointer path in `additionalModelResponseFieldPaths`.

blocks.prompt: Converse is a stateless call. Your chat app is on turn 5 of a conversation. What happens to `usage.inputTokens` from turn 1 to turn 5, and why?
blocks.reveal: It grows. The docs say you maintain context by including all the messages of the conversation in each subsequent request. Turn 5 resends turns 1 to 4 plus the new message, so you pay for (and spend quota on) the whole history every time. This is why long chats get slower and costlier, and why history trimming, summarization and prompt caching matter.

blocks.title: Dispatching on stopReason

scenes.caption: Call the model and read stopReason. The loop exists because one user turn can take several model calls.
The model asked for a tool. The assistant message (with its toolUse block) must be appended before the result.
Run the tool yourself and send its output back as a toolResult in a user message, then call again.
Second call ends normally: the answer is complete.
Other branches matter in production: max_tokens means the text was cut off; guardrail_intervened means a guardrail replaced the content.
ConverseStream returns a stream of events instead of one JSON body. First comes messageStart with the role.
Text arrives as contentBlockDelta events, each with a partial string and a contentBlockIndex to stitch blocks together.
messageStop carries the stopReason. Only after it do you know whether the answer is complete.
A final metadata event carries usage (token counts) and metrics (latency). Log it: it is your per-call cost record.

blocks.md: Converse unifies the **shape** of requests and responses, not the **behavior** of models. Models still differ in quality, context length, supported content types and tool support, which the docs list per model. A one-line modelId swap is easy; validating that the new model is good enough is still your job.
`inferenceConfig` has only four fields. Putting a model-specific parameter there is a mistake; it belongs in `additionalModelRequestFields`, and it only works for models that define it.

blocks.question: A response comes back with `stopReason` equal to `max_tokens` and the JSON your parser expected is missing its closing brace. What is the right first fix?
options: Lower temperature so the model writes less
Switch to ConverseStream, which has no output limit
Raise maxTokens (or shorten the requested output) and treat truncated replies as failures
Move maxTokens into additionalModelRequestFields
blocks.explain: max_tokens means generation hit the output cap you set, so the text was cut off. Raise the cap or ask for less, and make your code check stopReason before parsing. Streaming has the same cap, and maxTokens is a common inferenceConfig field.

blocks.question: Your team wants to A/B two foundation models from different providers with the least code change. Which design fits the Converse API best?
options: Keep one Converse call and pick modelId per request from config
Write one InvokeModel body builder per provider
Fine-tune both models first so their outputs match
Call both models through a knowledge base
blocks.explain: Converse keeps the request and response shape fixed across models that support messages, so the experiment is a config change of modelId. InvokeModel needs model-specific bodies.

lessons.title: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap

blocks.md:
**On-demand** inference means you share AWS-managed capacity and pay per token you actually use. To keep the shared pool fair, Bedrock enforces **quotas** per account and model. For text models the main ones are **tokens per minute (TPM)**, counting input and output, and tokens per day (TPD). Embedding models are the documented exception: they are throttled by requests per minute (RPM). Some text models also have a per-model RPM quota, and the TPD quota is shared across models per account.

Go over a quota and the call fails with a `ThrottlingException` (HTTP 429). Default values differ by account and change over time, so read them from the Service Quotas console instead of hard-coding them.

The surprise is *when* tokens are counted. The docs describe three stages:

1. **At the start** of a request, Bedrock deducts input tokens plus your `max_tokens` value, because it does not yet know how long the answer will be. If that exceeds the quota, the request is throttled.
2. **During** processing, the deduction is adjusted toward the real output count.
3. **At the end**, the final charge to the quota is computed and unused tokens are returned.

blocks.caption: Quota deduction per request. b is the model's output burndown rate; cache-read tokens do not count toward the quota.

blocks.md:
The **burndown rate** $b$ converts output tokens into quota usage. For most models it is 1, but the docs list higher rates for some models (their worked example uses 5, so one output token consumes 5 quota tokens). Burndown affects only the quota, not the bill: you are billed for actual tokens.

Now a worked example. These numbers are **illustrative**, not real quotas: a request with 2,000 input tokens that produces 300 output tokens on a model with $b = 5$, under a TPM quota of 200,000.

blocks.title: One request, four different token counts (illustrative)

scenes.caption: Billed tokens: 2,000 input + 300 output = 2,300. This is what the invoice sees.
Final quota usage: 2,000 + 5 x 300 = 3,500, because output burns down at 5x for this model.
Start-of-request deduction with max_tokens = 4,096: 2,000 + 4,096 = 6,096, nearly twice the final usage.
With max_tokens = 400 (still above the 300 actually needed) the start deduction drops to 2,400.

blocks.prompt: Illustrative: 40 of these requests arrive at the same moment against a 200,000 TPM quota. With `max_tokens` = 4,096, how many get in before the rest are throttled? And with 400?
blocks.reveal: With 4,096 each request reserves 6,096 tokens up front, and 200,000 / 6,096 = 32.8, so only **32** are admitted (simplified: we treat all 40 as in flight at once). With 400 each reserves 2,400, 40 x 2,400 = 96,000, so **all 40** fit. Yet each request settles at the same 3,500 either way, so all 40 together would use only 140,000, well under the quota. An oversized max_tokens throttles you for capacity you never use.

blocks.md: Set `max_tokens` close to the longest answer you really need. The AWS docs say it directly: if you hit TPM quotas earlier than expected, reduce max_tokens to better approximate your completions. Measure real output lengths from the `OutputTokenCount` metric.

Other documented levers when on-demand capacity is tight:

- **Cross-Region inference.** Call an *inference profile* instead of a single-Region model ID. A geographic profile routes within a geography (for example US or EU), a global profile across supported commercial Regions. The docs say there is no extra routing cost and that data stays on the AWS network. Choose geographic profiles when data residency matters.
- **Prompt caching.** Cache-read tokens do not count toward the quota.
- **Service tiers.** The docs list [four tiers](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/service-tiers-inference.html): Reserved (reserved capacity), Priority (faster, at a premium), Standard (the default) and Flex (cheaper, slower). Priority, Standard and Flex share your on-demand quota; Reserved is separate.
- **Retries with backoff** on 429, since throttling is expected behavior, not an outage.
Specific burndown rates, default quotas and tier prices change as models launch. Treat any number you remember as stale and read the current quota page and model card before you size a workload.

blocks.question: Your app sends 1,000 input tokens and gets about 100 output tokens back on a model with burndown 5. Monitoring shows TPM throttling even though the per-minute *billed* tokens are far below the quota. Which change helps most?
options: Raise temperature to shorten answers
Lower max_tokens from 8,192 to about 200
Switch from Converse to InvokeModel
Split each prompt into two smaller requests
blocks.explain: The start-of-request deduction is input + max_tokens = 9,192 per call, about 6x the final 1,500 (1,000 + 5 x 100). Right-sizing max_tokens frees that reserved headroom. The API choice does not change quota math, and splitting prompts adds overhead.

blocks.question: Which statement about the output burndown rate is correct according to the AWS docs?
options: It multiplies your bill for output tokens
It applies to cache-read tokens only
It is always 5 for every model
It affects how fast output tokens consume the TPM quota, but you are billed for actual tokens
blocks.explain: The docs give an example of 1,000 input and 100 output tokens at 5x burndown: 1,500 tokens leave the quota, but you are billed for 1,100. Most models have a 1:1 rate unless the model card says otherwise.

lessons.title: Provisioned Throughput: when buying capacity beats paying per token

blocks.md:
**Provisioned Throughput** buys dedicated capacity for one model at a fixed hourly price. You buy it in **Model Units (MUs)**. The docs define an MU by two numbers: how many input tokens it can process, and how many output tokens it can generate, across all requests in one minute. The per-MU throughput and price depend on the model and are not published as a table; the docs say to contact your AWS account manager.

You choose a commitment: none (delete any time), 1 month or 6 months. Longer commitments get a lower hourly price, and billing continues until you delete it.

Why does this exist when on-demand is simpler?

- **Guaranteed capacity.** On-demand shares a pool and throttles at your quota; provisioned capacity is yours, which AWS positions as consistent performance and lower latency.
- **Custom models.** A customized model needs somewhere to run. The docs offer Provisioned Throughput or, for supported base models, an on-demand custom model deployment.
- **Cost at high, steady utilization.** A fixed hourly price wins when the capacity is busy most of the time.

One constraint to remember: the docs say inference profiles (cross-Region inference) do not support Provisioned Throughput.

A worked example with **illustrative** numbers only (cost units, cu, not real prices). A support assistant uses 2,000 input and 300 output tokens per request. Traffic is 40 requests per minute for 12 busy hours and 5 per minute for 12 quiet hours.

- Requests per day: 12 x 60 x 40 + 12 x 60 x 5 = 32,400.
- Tokens per day: 64.8M input, 9.72M output.
- On-demand at 4 cu per 1M input and 20 cu per 1M output: 259.2 + 194.4 = **453.6 cu/day**.
- Peak needs 80,000 input and 12,000 output tokens per minute. If one MU gives 50,000 input and 7,500 output TPM, peak needs 1.6 MUs, so you buy **2 MUs**. At 8 cu per MU-hour: 2 x 24 x 8 = **384 cu/day**.

blocks.title: Daily cost of the same workload (illustrative cost units)

scenes.caption: On-demand: you pay only for tokens used, 453.6 cu per day at today's traffic.
Provisioned: 2 MUs sized for the busy-hour peak cost 384 cu per day whether busy or idle. Here it is cheaper.
Halve the traffic: on-demand drops to 226.8 cu, while provisioned still needs 1 MU (192 cu). Still cheaper, but only barely.
Quarter traffic: on-demand 113.4 cu versus a 1 MU floor of 192 cu. Now provisioned capacity sits mostly idle and loses.

blocks.md: The cleanest way to see the tradeoff is **utilization**. Average input load is 64.8M / 1,440 minutes = 45,000 TPM against 100,000 TPM of capacity, so the MUs are 45% utilized. A fully busy MU-hour would cost, at on-demand rates, 60 x (50,000 x 4 + 7,500 x 20) / 1M = 21 cu. Provisioned wins when utilization beats the ratio of its hourly price to that value.

blocks.tex: u^{*} = \frac{\text{price per MU-hour}}{\text{on-demand cost of a fully used MU-hour}} = \frac{8}{21} \approx 0.38
blocks.caption: Breakeven utilization (illustrative). Our workload runs at 0.45, above 0.38, so provisioned is cheaper. Simplified: assumes the input to output mix matches the MU's ratio.

scenes.caption: At today's traffic (x = 1) provisioned (2 MUs) undercuts on-demand. The staircase is the MU count stepping up as peak demand grows.
Below x of about 0.42 the 1-MU floor costs more than on-demand. Each new MU also opens a gap (x from 0.63 to 0.85 here) where on-demand wins again: low or bursty traffic favors paying per token.
Raise the MU-hour price to 12 (a shorter commitment, say): now provisioned never beats on-demand at any traffic level, because utilization never reaches the 12 / 21 = 0.57 breakeven.

blocks.code:
import math
in_tok, out_tok = 2000, 300                  # per request
reqs = 12*60*40 + 12*60*5                    # 32,400 per day
od = reqs*in_tok/1e6*4 + reqs*out_tok/1e6*20 # 453.6 cu/day
mu_in, mu_out, mu_hr = 50_000, 7_500, 8      # illustrative MU
mus = math.ceil(max(40*in_tok/mu_in, 40*out_tok/mu_out))  # 2
prov = mus*24*mu_hr                          # 384 cu/day
util = reqs*in_tok/1440/(mus*mu_in)          # 0.45
full = 60*(mu_in*4 + mu_out*20)/1e6          # 21 cu per busy MU-hour
print(od, prov, util, mu_hr/full)            # breakeven 0.38
blocks.caption: The script behind every number in this lesson. All prices and MU sizes are made up for teaching.

blocks.md: Provisioned capacity must cover your **peak**, so spiky traffic lowers utilization and erodes the savings. Also, provisioned capacity does not overflow anywhere by itself; plan what happens above it (queueing, on-demand fallback) as part of the design.

blocks.question: Using the illustrative numbers, traffic grows to 2x today. Peak input becomes 160,000 TPM. How many MUs do you need, and which option is cheaper per day?
options: 4 MUs; provisioned (768 cu) beats on-demand (907.2 cu)
3 MUs; provisioned (576 cu) beats on-demand
4 MUs; on-demand is cheaper
2 MUs are still enough because average load is lower
blocks.explain: 160,000 / 50,000 = 3.2 and 24,000 / 7,500 = 3.2, so you need ceil(3.2) = 4 MUs: 4 x 24 x 8 = 768 cu. On-demand doubles to 907.2 cu. Capacity is sized to peak, not average.

blocks.question: Which change to the same total daily token volume makes Provisioned Throughput **more** attractive?
options: Concentrating all traffic into a 2-hour burst
Raising max_tokens
Spreading traffic evenly across 24 hours
Moving to a global inference profile
blocks.explain: Provisioned capacity is sized to peak. Flat traffic lowers the peak for the same volume, so fewer MUs run at higher utilization. A burst does the opposite. Inference profiles do not support Provisioned Throughput at all.

lessons.title: Customizing models: fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining and import

blocks.md:
Prompting and retrieval change what the model *sees*. **Customization** changes the model's *weights*. Bedrock documents several managed paths, and the right one depends on what data you have:

- **Supervised fine-tuning**: labeled input and output pairs teach the task.
- **Reinforcement fine-tuning**: no labeled outputs; you supply reward functions (for example as AWS Lambda functions) that score responses, and the model learns from those scores.
- **Distillation**: a larger *teacher* model's answers train a smaller, cheaper *student*.
- **Continued pre-training**: unlabeled domain text (an AWS launch post says each record needs only an input, no completion) extends what the model knows. The current customization overview lists only the first three; the API still accepts `CONTINUED_PRE_TRAINING` as a job type.

Training is charged by tokens processed (corpus tokens x epochs) plus monthly model storage.

blocks.title: Pick a customization path from the data you have

scenes.caption: Start from your data, not from the technique. Each question leads to a different managed job.
Labeled prompt and answer pairs: supervised fine-tuning.
Only prompts plus a way to score answers: reinforcement fine-tuning with reward functions.
Prompts, and a big model that already does the task well: distill it into a smaller student. Bedrock generates teacher answers, or reuses them from invocation logs.
A large unlabeled domain corpus: continued pre-training. Weights trained elsewhere (for example on SageMaker AI): Custom Model Import.
Every path ends in a custom model you must serve: Provisioned Throughput, or an on-demand deployment where the docs support it.

blocks.md:
**Where LoRA fits.** Recall from the LoRA course that LoRA freezes the base weights and trains small low-rank adapter matrices. The Bedrock customization overview does not expose a LoRA switch. LoRA appears in the documented path for customizing Amazon Nova models on **SageMaker AI**: the training recipe has a `peft_scheme` setting where `"lora"` selects LoRA PEFT and `null` runs full-rank fine-tuning.

The AWS launch post for that feature states the serving consequence: PEFT-adapted Nova models are imported to Bedrock and invoked with **on-demand** inference, while fully fine-tuned ones run with **Provisioned Throughput**. Small adapters on a shared base are cheap to serve per token; a full copy of changed weights needs dedicated capacity.

blocks.prompt: You have 200,000 production prompts already answered by a large model and logged through Bedrock invocation logging. You want a cheaper model for this task. What is the least work path, and is there a catch?
blocks.reveal: **Distillation using invocation logs.** The docs let a distillation job read prompt and response pairs straight from invocation logs, optionally filtered by the `requestMetadata` you attached to each call. The catch: the teacher model named in the job must match the model in the logs, or the logs are not used. If you let Bedrock synthesize extra teacher responses instead, those teacher calls are billed at on-demand rates.

blocks.md:
**Custom Model Import** brings weights you trained elsewhere. You upload Hugging Face format files to Amazon S3: `.safetensors` weights, `config.json` and tokenizer files. The model must be one of the documented open architectures (families such as Llama, Mistral and Qwen are listed), and the import job detects the architecture.

Imported models run on demand. Bedrock decides how many **Custom Model Units (CMUs)** one copy of your model needs, and it scales the number of running copies with demand. Billing runs in 5-minute windows from the first successful call.

blocks.caption: Custom Model Import cost, as in the AWS pricing page example (rate per CMU-minute x 5 minutes x active windows). Each 5-minute window is billed for the copies running in it; more copies under load means proportionally more cost.

blocks.md: Serving rules for custom models have changed over time. A 2023 AWS launch post said custom models needed Provisioned Throughput; current docs also offer on-demand custom model deployments, but only for listed base models and Regions. Check the current page before you promise a serving cost.

blocks.question: Your team has 50,000 labeled support tickets with ideal replies and wants a model that matches the house style. Which documented path fits best?
options: Continued pre-training on the tickets
Supervised fine-tuning on ticket and reply pairs
Reinforcement fine-tuning with no reward function
Intelligent Prompt Routing
blocks.explain: Labeled input and output pairs are exactly what supervised fine-tuning uses. Continued pre-training takes unlabeled text and would not learn the reply mapping. Reinforcement fine-tuning needs reward functions. Routing does not change any model.

blocks.question: Why would a LoRA-adapted model be cheaper to serve on demand than a fully fine-tuned one, in the AWS Nova customization flow?
options: LoRA models have fewer layers
LoRA removes the need for a tokenizer
Full fine-tunes cannot be imported into Bedrock
Only small adapter weights differ from the shared base, so the AWS post says PEFT models run on demand while full fine-tunes use Provisioned Throughput
blocks.explain: The adapters are small and the base is shared, so per-token on-demand serving works. A full fine-tune changes every weight, which needs its own dedicated copy. The AWS post says full fine-tunes can also be imported, but they run with Provisioned Throughput.

lessons.title: Building blocks: routing, prompt optimization, RAG, agents, guardrails

blocks.md:
Beyond the inference call, Bedrock offers managed building blocks. This lesson covers what each one does, as documented, so you can recognize it in an architecture. Routing, RAG and guardrails each have their own deeper course.

**Intelligent Prompt Routing** gives you one endpoint in front of models *from the same family*. For each request it predicts the response quality of each model and routes accordingly. You set a **fallback model** and a **response quality difference**: with 10% and a small fallback model, the docs say the router switches to the larger model only if its predicted quality is more than 10% better. You call it by passing the router ARN as `modelId`; the response's `trace.promptRouter.invokedModelId` tells you which model answered.

Documented limits of routing: it is optimized for English prompts, it cannot learn from your application-specific performance data, and how well it works depends on its initial training data.

**Prompt optimization** (`OptimizePrompt`) rewrites one prompt for one target model. The simple mode is a fast heuristic rewrite that works best on prompts of roughly 1k tokens or less; it streams an `analyzePromptEvent` and then an `optimizedPromptEvent`. AWS also documents an advanced, evaluation-driven mode across several models.

**Knowledge Bases** are managed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). At ingestion, documents are split into chunks, embedded and written to a vector index. At query time the question is embedded, similar chunks are retrieved and added to the prompt. `RetrieveAndGenerate` does retrieval plus generation and returns **citations**; `Retrieve` returns chunks only. The docs distinguish managed knowledge bases from customer-managed ones where you run the vector store.

**Agents** orchestrate a model, *action groups* (APIs the agent may call) and knowledge bases. Note the docs now mark Bedrock Agents as *Agents Classic*, closed to new customers, and point to **Amazon Bedrock AgentCore** instead.

**Guardrails** are configurable filters (harmful content, denied topics, words, sensitive information, grounding checks). Attach one to a Converse call with `guardrailConfig`, or call `ApplyGuardrail` on any text.

blocks.title: Composing the blocks into one request path

scenes.caption: The bare call: app to model. Everything else is optional and composable.
Add a guardrail on the way in: harmful or off-topic prompts are blocked before any model tokens are spent.
Add a knowledge base: retrieved chunks with citations are added to the prompt.
Replace the fixed model with a prompt router: easy prompts go to the smaller model, hard ones to the larger.
Finally a guardrail on the way out checks the response (for example grounding against the retrieved chunks) before the user sees it.

blocks.md: Each block also adds latency and its own cost line (router, retrieval, guardrail units). Start with the bare call, measure, and add a block only when it fixes a measured problem.

blocks.question: You configure a prompt router with a small fallback model, a larger second model and a response quality difference of 10%. For a given prompt, the router predicts the larger model would be 6% better. Where does the request go?
options: The larger model, because it is predicted to be better
Both models, and the better answer is returned
The fallback (small) model, because 6% is below the 10% criterion
It is rejected with a validation error
blocks.explain: The fallback model is the anchor. The router switches away from it only when the other model's predicted quality beats it by more than the configured difference.

blocks.question: A user reports a wrong answer from your RAG app built on RetrieveAndGenerate. What in the response helps you debug it first?
options: The citations, which map parts of the answer to retrieved source chunks
usage.outputTokens
The guardrail trace only
stopReason
blocks.explain: Citations tie spans of the generated answer to retrieved references, so you can see whether retrieval found the wrong chunks or the model misread the right ones.

lessons.title: Below the API: Inferentia, Trainium, Neuron and SageMaker AI

blocks.md:
Managed APIs hide the hardware. When you run models yourself on AWS, you choose it, and besides GPUs AWS designs its own ML chips:

- **AWS Inferentia** is built for inference. AWS calls Inferentia2 its second-generation inference accelerator; it powers Inf2 instances.
- **AWS Trainium** is aimed at both training and inference at scale, according to AWS. Generations include Trainium (Trn1), Trainium2 (Trn2) and Trainium3.

These chips are programmed through the **AWS Neuron SDK**, not CUDA. Neuron includes a compiler (`neuronx-cc`) that turns framework models into device code, a runtime that loads and runs them and handles collective communication, PyTorch support (TorchNeuron) and JAX support through a PJRT plugin, vLLM Neuron for LLM serving, and the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) for writing custom kernels.

Inside the chip, the unit of compute is a **NeuronCore**. The Neuron docs describe NeuronCore-v2 (used in Inferentia2 and Trainium) as four engines plus on-chip SRAM that the **compiler** manages:

- **Tensor engine**: a systolic array for matrix multiply, convolution and transpose.
- **Vector engine**: operations where each output depends on many inputs, such as layer normalization and pooling.
- **Scalar engine**: element-wise operations where each output depends on one input element, such as activation functions.
- **GPSIMD engine**: general-purpose programmable vector processors for custom operators written in C.

blocks.title: One transformer layer on a NeuronCore-v2 (simplified)

scenes.caption: Weights and activations live in device HBM. The compiler stages tiles into on-chip SRAM, close to the engines.
The Q, K, V and MLP projections are matrix multiplies, so they run on the Tensor engine (systolic array).
Layer norm and softmax reduce over many values per output, so they map to the Vector engine.
An element-wise activation touches each value once: the Scalar engine.
An unusual op with no built-in mapping can be written as a custom operator on GPSIMD. Simplified: the real compiler also overlaps engines and DMA transfers.

blocks.md: Generation to generation, the Neuron docs publish chip specs. Trainium2 has eight NeuronCore-v3 cores, 96 GiB of HBM at 2.9 TB/s, and 667 dense BF16 TFLOPS (1,299 in FP8). Trainium1 had 32 GiB at 0.8 TB/s and 191 BF16 TFLOPS. For comparison, an [Inferentia2](https://awsdocs-neuron.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/general/arch/neuron-hardware/inferentia2.html) chip has two NeuronCore-v2 cores and 32 GiB of HBM.

scenes.caption: Trainium1 as the baseline: every metric set to 1.
Trainium2 ratios computed from the Neuron spec tables (the docs round slightly differently). FP8 compute grew most.
Note that BF16 compute grew 3.49x while HBM bandwidth grew 3.62x: the balance between math and memory stayed roughly similar.

blocks.prompt: Recall the roofline idea from GPU basics. Trainium2 offers 667 BF16 TFLOPS and 2.9 TB/s of HBM bandwidth per chip. How many FLOPs per byte must a kernel do to be compute bound, and where does batch-1 LLM decoding land?
blocks.reveal: 667e12 / 2.9e12 is about **230 FLOPs per byte**. Batch-1 decoding reads each BF16 weight (2 bytes) once and does about 2 FLOPs with it (a multiply and an add), about 1 FLOP per byte, far below 230. So decoding is memory-bandwidth bound on this chip just as on GPUs, which is why batching, KV caching and quantization matter on any accelerator.

blocks.md:
**SageMaker AI versus Bedrock.** Amazon SageMaker AI is AWS's managed service to build, train and deploy ML models where *you* choose the model, container and instance types. Its inference options include real-time endpoints, serverless endpoints and asynchronous endpoints, with autoscaling. Neuron is integrated with SageMaker, so the Inferentia or Trainium instances can sit behind those endpoints.

Bedrock is the opposite end: serverless model APIs priced per token or per Model Unit, where AWS runs the hardware. The usual split for an applied scientist: Bedrock to use and lightly customize hosted models fast; SageMaker AI (or EC2) when you need your own architecture, training loop, kernels or hardware choice.

Moving work onto Inferentia or Trainium is a **compiler** project as much as a hardware choice: your model must compile with Neuron, and custom ops may need NKI kernels. Budget engineering time for that, not just instance price.

blocks.question: A layer normalization in your model is slow on a NeuronCore. Which engine is it documented to map to?
options: Tensor engine
Vector engine
Scalar engine
The host CPU
blocks.explain: The Neuron docs list layer normalization and pooling as Vector engine work: each output depends on many inputs. The Tensor engine is for matrix-style work and the Scalar engine for one-input-per-output operations.

blocks.question: Your team built a new attention variant with custom kernels and wants to train it from scratch. Which AWS layer fits best?
options: A Bedrock Knowledge Base
Bedrock supervised fine-tuning
SageMaker AI or EC2 training on GPU or Trainium instances, with Neuron if on Trainium
Intelligent Prompt Routing
blocks.explain: Bedrock customization adapts supported base models; it does not run your own architecture from scratch. Self-managed training on SageMaker AI or EC2 gives you the code, kernels and hardware choice. Afterwards, Custom Model Import could serve it if its architecture is supported.
